latestRelease.title: v1.65.0/v0.159.0
latestRelease.notes:
### Images and binaries here: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-releases/releases/tag/v0.159.0

## End User Changelog

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `pkg/exporterhelper`: Add the `pkg.exporterhelper.queueBatchEnabled` feature gate (#14038, #13582, #12022)
  When enabled, the batch settings returned by `NewDefaultQueueConfig()` have
  `batch::enabled` true. See [migration RFC](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/docs/rfcs/batching-migration.md#phase-1).
  

### 🧰 Bug fixes 🧰

- `pkg/exporterhelper`: Record `otelcol_exporter_queue_batch_send_size` and `otelcol_exporter_queue_batch_send_size_bytes` after batching, and add `otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size` and `otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size_bytes` for enqueue-time sizes. (#14674)
  Previously the batch send size histograms were recorded at enqueue time (`Offer`), so they
  measured incoming request sizes rather than the post-batching request handed to the
  downstream sender. Those histograms are now recorded in the obs report sender.
  The previous enqueue-time measurements are preserved under the new
  `otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size` and `otelcol_exporter_enqueue_size_bytes` metrics for
  queue sizing. Users with the exporter batcher enabled will observe different values for
  `otelcol_exporter_queue_batch_send_size*`.
  `otelcol_exporter_queue_batch_send_size` and `otelcol_exporter_queue_batch_send_size_bytes`
  are now only recorded when `sending_queue::batch` is configured; they will not appear at all
  for exporters that do not enable batching.
  
- `pkg/scraperhelper`: Use `{record}` instead of `{datapoint}` as the unit of the log record and profile record scraper metrics (#15730)
  Affects `otelcol_scraper_scraped_log_records`, `otelcol_scraper_errored_log_records`,
  `otelcol_scraper_scraped_profile_records` and `otelcol_scraper_errored_profile_records`.

signals.title: Add queue-oriented storage interface for persistent queues
signals.text: ### Component(s) exporter/exporterhelper ### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe. When setting up persistent queues, we use `file_storage` as the mechanism to store in-flight data. This is backed by a bbolt database. [Like others](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/44469), we have had stability issues caused by excessive bbolt memory usage when using this configuration. Our main issue occurs at startup when queues are large (100GB+), but there are various incarnations of the problem where bbolt will use excessive memory, leading to OOMKills. When trying to build our own replacement that does not use bbolt, we quickly ran into a design issue preventing resolution of the problem. The current [storage.Client](https://pkg.go.dev/go.opentelemetry.io/collector/extension/xextension/storage#section-readme) interface used for persistent queuing is key/value oriented. When implementing a storage provider, one must support random access by key. This design requires a storage provider to have some form of indexing (to efficiently find the key) and a data structure that can support random sets and deletes by key. With queues that may exceed 100GB (the need for these large queues is out of our control), indexing not only requires extra disk and reduces performance, but its also unnecessary. We'd simply like to store events in a FIFO-like queue and retrieve them later. As an added benefit, FIFO operations would be roughly constant time and would not get slower as the queue increases in size. ### Describe the solution you'd like In addition to the current key/value interface, I'd like to propose a secondary interface that implements a proper queue abstraction. Rather than get/set/delete, we'd use a FIFO interface. To illustrate the concept at a high level, this would be something like: ```go type QueueClient interface { Close(ctx context.Context) error // Offer appends one item to the durable tail of the queue. Offer(ctx context.Context, value []byte) error // Reserve claims the next item from the durable head of the queue for // processing. The item remains durable until Ack is called with the returned // ID. If the process crashes or the reservation expires, the item should // become eligible for reservation again. Reserve(ctx context.Context, lease LeaseOptions) (QueueEntryID, []byte, error) // Ack permanently completes a reserved item. Ack(ctx context.Context, id QueueEntryID) error // Nack releases a reserved item back to the queue without completing it. Nack(ctx context.Context, id QueueEntryID) error } ``` Under the hood, we'd write the events to segmented files. Once all the events in a segment have been acked, we'd reclaim that segment. ### Describe alternatives you've considered It may be possible to implement an on-disk queue and use sqlite or something for key to queue entry ID bookkeeping, but introducing a queue-oriented extension interface avoids the additional overhead associated with that mapping. ### Additional context _No response_ ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

signals.title: pprofileotlp.ExportRequest does not use the ProfilesDictionary for Resource attributes
signals.text: ### Component(s) pdata/pprofile ### What happened? **Describe the bug** `pprofileotlp.ExportRequest` serializes `ms.orig` directly rather than delegating to the `pprofile` marshalers: ```go func (ms ExportRequest) MarshalProto() ([]byte, error) { size := ms.orig.SizeProto() buf := make([]byte, size) _ = ms.orig.MarshalProto(buf) return buf, nil } ``` So `convertProfilesToReferences` never runs on marshal, and `resolveProfilesReferences` never runs on unmarshal (same for the JSON pair). The reference-based attribute support added in #14546 therefore does not apply on the OTLP export path, the path the OTLP receiver and exporter actually use. **Steps to reproduce** ```go pd := pprofile.NewProfiles() pd.Dictionary().StringTable().Append("") // index 0 must be the empty sentinel rp := pd.ResourceProfiles().AppendEmpty() rp.Resource().Attributes().PutStr("service.name", "checkout") rp.ScopeProfiles().AppendEmpty() pd.MarkReadOnly() // so the first marshal copies instead of mutating pd viaPprofile, _ := (&pprofile.ProtoMarshaler{}).MarshalProfiles(pd) viaExportReq, _ := pprofileotlp.NewExportRequestFromProfiles(pd).MarshalProto() var a profilesv1.ProfilesData proto.Unmarshal(viaPprofile, &a) var b collectorprofilesv1.ExportProfilesServiceRequest proto.Unmarshal(viaExportReq, &b) fmt.Printf("pprofile.ProtoMarshaler string_table=%q (%d bytes)\n", a.GetDictionary().GetStringTable(), len(viaPprofile)) fmt.Printf("ExportRequest.MarshalProto string_table=%q (%d bytes)\n", b.GetDictionary().GetStringTable(), len(viaExportReq)) ``` **What did you expect to see?** Both encodings referencing the attribute key and string value through the dictionary string table. **What did you see instead?** ``` pprofile.ProtoMarshaler string_table=["" "service.name" "checkout"] (44 bytes) ExportRequest.MarshalProto string_table=[""] (40 bytes) ``` The `ExportRequest` encoding leaves string_table untouched and inlines the attribute (`key="service.name"`, k`ey_strindex=0`). Two marshalers of the same `Profiles` produce different wire encodings, and the dictionary wire-size benefit is lost on the export path. ### Collector version v0.159.0
signals.author: nsavoire

signals.title: Unset key_strindex is treated as a reference to string_table[0], erasing inline attribute keys
signals.text: ### Component(s) pdata/pprofile ### What happened? **Describe the bug** `resolveKeyValueReferences` in `pdata/pprofile/dictionary_helpers.go` treats `key_strindex == 0` as a valid reference: ```go if kv.KeyStrindex >= 0 { idx := int(kv.KeyStrindex) if idx < dict.StringTable().Len() { kv.Key = dict.StringTable().At(idx) ``` But `0` is the "not set" sentinel, so for any producer that sends attribute keys inline the key is silently replaced with `""` on unmarshal. **Steps to reproduce** ```go msg := &profilesv1.ProfilesData{ ResourceProfiles: []*profilesv1.ResourceProfiles{{ Resource: &resourcev1.Resource{Attributes: []*commonv1.KeyValue{{ Key: "service.name", Value: &commonv1.AnyValue{Value: &commonv1.AnyValue_StringValue{StringValue: "checkout"}}, }}}, ScopeProfiles: []*profilesv1.ScopeProfiles{{}}, }}, Dictionary: &profilesv1.ProfilesDictionary{StringTable: []string{""}}, } wire, _ := proto.Marshal(msg) pd, _ := (&pprofile.ProtoUnmarshaler{}).UnmarshalProfiles(wire) fmt.Println(pd.ResourceProfiles().At(0).Resource().Attributes().AsRaw()) ``` **What did you expect to see?** `map[service.name:checkout]` **What did you see instead?** `map[:checkout]`: the attribute key is gone. ### Collector version v0.159.0 ### Environment information _No response_ ### OpenTelemetry Collector configuration ```yaml ``` ### Log output ```shell ``` ### Additional context Related: `key_strindex` is also not cleared after resolution. The code intentionally keeps it set ("N.b. keep KeyStrindex set to optimize re-marshaling. This is technically a violation of the proto spec"), but this seems dangerous: any serialization path that does not run `convertKeyValueToReferences` emits both fileds onto the wire. `pprofileotlp.ExportRequest.MarshalProto` is such a path (see #15792). Moreover the optimization that jusitified this has been removed by #15134. ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

signals.title: [cmd/mdatagen] Versioned Metrics migration improve documentation template
signals.text: ### Component(s) cmd/mdatagen ### Describe the issue you're reporting Currently in mdatagen when we generate documentation for a component that is using the versioned metrics migration path we get the following test: ```text When the disable-old gate is enabled, emission of this metric is suppressed. When the enable-new gate is enabled, the target metric is emitted. If both gates are disabled, only this metric is emitted; if both are enabled, only the target metric is emitted. ``` Text is located [here](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/b6918236de851afd9fbf560d43c44909a0fbf4e8/cmd/mdatagen/internal/templates/documentation.md.tmpl?plain=1#L41). It has been pointed out in hostmetrics receiver pull-request that this could be improved, see [here](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/pull/49987#discussion_r3820356858). It might be easier to read if we have a table to explain, something like: Emission depends on the state of the two migration feature gates: | `{{ $metric.Migration.ThroughGates.EnableNew }}` | `{{ $metric.Migration.ThroughGates.DisableOld }}` | Emitted metric(s) | | --- | --- | --- | | disabled | disabled | `{{ $metricName }}` only | | enabled | disabled | `{{ $metricName }}` and `{{ $metric.Migration.To }}` | | enabled | enabled | `{{ $metric.Migration.To }}` only | | disabled | enabled | Migrated metrics: none (v0 suppressed, v1 gated off — warnings logged). Non-migrated metrics still emit. No startup error. | ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. signals.title: queuestorage: A storage extension optimized for queues based on bbolt.
signals.text: ### Component(s) exporter/exporterhelper ### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe. For exporterhelper queue, we have filestorage extension which has multiple performance issue like Process Memory shootup and high disk i/o consumption by bbolt DB when queue size is large. These are the same issues already listed in https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/15384 and https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/44469 . ### Describe the solution you'd like An enhanced version of bbolt which is purely optimized for queue use case. All performance issues arises when bbolt database gets large and b-tree and mmap grows. We can use segmented access pattern. Since it's for queue based extension, say queue_storage extension where we know we know that we don't need all keys to be loaded by bbolt, since we know queue consumption will be sequential, we can leverage that to create sequential segment db files. Segment-per-bbolt design Example: When say, 64MB is the segment limit. This can be made configurable. ``` storage-dir/ seg_000000000000.db ← oldest active segment (items 0–1000 , sizne ~64MB) seg_000000001000.db ← next segment (items 1000–1999, size ~64MB) seg_000000002000.db ← current write segment (...) qmv0 metadata key same as existing filestorage. ``` Each seg_*.db is a normal bbolt database, but holds only the items for that slice of the queue. The filename encodes the starting write index of that segment so you can route any key to its segment in O(1). In reality, we need to open a new segment DB file only after consuming all items for previous segment. Also we would need to open 2 segment files at any time , one to enqueue(most latest segment file) and one to dequeue(Can be any from segment file which is actively being read..). In this way, otel process will open atmost 2 segment DB files at anytime even for a very large queue backlog. This makes memory config/growth very predictable(~124MB for 2 segment files). Also since a single read segment loaded is memory bounded(64Mb default), we can reduce random disk access by preloading the 64MB data pages sequentially into OS cache and when bbolt needs a ramdom page traversing B-tree index, it finds it in OS cache rather than making a Disk i/o. This concept is tested in below attached doc and an impressive ~8x read speed improvement and reduced disk iops was observed. This feature request is a fork from https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/15384#issuecomment-5100729005 I have implemented the same to do a POC and capture the testing and performance benchmarks in [this doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TsrdIhJpU2kica8rsA8nnQaYUVvPr11F7Z_QqjGkO80/edit?tab=t.0) [Draft implementation](https://github.com/jagan2221/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/extension/storage/queuestorage) of queuestorage extension. This implementation contains the core implementations for now for doing a POC. Cosmetic changes and config related things like ensuring all the required configs and defaults are yet to be done based on approval. **List of performance related issue we have with filestorage extension vs How segmented approach solves this.** **Segmented BBolt vs Single BBolt — Improvements Summary** **1. Bounded Memory Usage** Single DB mmaps the entire file — a 50GB queue means 50GB of virtual memory pressure, leading to OOM kills under memory limits. Segmented approach only mmaps 2-3 open segments (128-192 MiB) regardless of total queue size. **2. Instant Space Reclamation** In single DB, deleted items remain as freelist pages — the file never shrinks without expensive compaction. In segmented, once all items in a segment are acked, os.Remove() deletes the file instantly. Disk space is freed in real-time as consumers catch up. **3. Fast Startup** Single DB must reconstruct the freelist by scanning the entire B-tree on open — 30GB file takes 30-60 seconds. Segmented opens only 1 segment file (~100ms) and reads metadata. Startup time is constant regardless of queue history. **4. Low Disk I/O Thrashing** A 64MB segment fits entirely in the OS page cache. All reads within a segment are memory accesses with zero page faults. Single large DB's B-tree index pages are scattered across the entire file and get evicted under memory pressure, causing 5-6 random IOPs per read. **5. No Compaction Overhead** Single DB requires periodic compaction to reclaim space — this copies the entire live dataset to a new file, consuming heavy CPU, IOPS, and temporary disk space (2x). Segmented never needs compaction — segment deletion is the GC mechanism. Zero background CPU, zero IOPS wasted on maintenance. **6. Predictable Tail Latency** Compaction in single DB causes latency spikes (write stalls while DB is being copied/reopened). Segmented has no such stalls — every operation has consistent latency since there's no background maintenance competing for resources. **7. Better IOPS Budget Utilization** For IOPS bounded machines, Like a VM running on AWS with gp3 (3000 IOPS baseline) for storage, single DB startup can saturate the entire IOPS budget for 30-60 seconds (scanning freelist). Segmented startup consumes less IOPs. ### Describe alternatives you've considered Wanted to try a different DB like pebble, which is as LSM based storage, but initial thoughts about the use case which is data written will be deleted very quickly and new data will be enqueued. this kind of high throughtput short lived data could potentially be expensive because of tombstones and old SSTables eventually need compaction. Also when thought about enhancing bbolt, i felt enhanced bbolt will perform much better to address the performance limitations which we have currently given it's already time tested with filestorage extension. ### Additional context _No response_ ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

signals.title: [chore][rfc/confmap]: add two new approaches for merging lists across configurations
signals.text: Following up on my meeting with @mx-psi, @dmitryax and @evan-bradley, I'm adding two more approaches we discussed during the meet for `docs/rfcs/configuration-merging-strategy.md`. 1. Specifying the lists to merge via command line flags: - This approach adds separate top-level CLI flags to control the merging behaviour. 2. Specifying the lists to merge in the configuration itself: - This approac uses a dedicated top-level `merge:` section that declares which paths in *that file* should be merged into the running configuration
signals.author: VihasMakwana

signals.title: [confignet] Allow setting security descriptors for npipes
signals.text: #### Description Add `dialer.security_descriptor` field to set an SDDL security descriptor on Windows named pipe (npipe) listeners in confignet. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15211 #### Testing Added unit tests which actually create the named pipe with specified descriptors. #### Documentation Documented the field in the struct definition, the schema, and the readme.
signals.author: swiatekm

signals.title: [confighttp] Move keepalive config into a dedicated optional section
signals.text: #### Description Move the keepalive-related options into a dedicated optional section. We go from: ```yaml endpoint: "http://localhost:4318" idle_conn_timeout: 90s max_idle_conns: 100 max_idle_conns_per_host: 10 ``` to: ```yaml endpoint: "http://localhost:4318" keepalive: idle_conn_timeout: 90s max_idle_conns: 100 max_idle_conns_per_host: 10 ``` The old configuration still exists and works. We fail validation if both are set. The implementation is somewhat complex and tries to minimize breakage across multiple scenarios. It proceeds by standardizing on the old, deprecated fields in `Unmarshal` and nulling the new section. See comments on the `Unmarshal` implementation and compatibility tests in `keepalive_compat_tests.go`. The most notable scenario that doesn't work goes like this: ```go cfg := NewDefaultClientConfig() conf.Unmarshal(cfg) cfg.KeepAlive = nil client := cfg.ToClient() ``` Keepalives will be enabled for such a client. This, and other limitations, exist as tests in `keepalive_compat_test.go`. Their intent is to show how a given implementation fares, in case somebody can come up with a better one. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/14020 #### Testing Added unit tests for all the new functions and some more generic unmarshalling tests. I've also added compatibility tests in `keepalive_compat_test.go` which assert that typical use cases from contrib still work as expected, and also show the limitations of this approach. I'm open to dropping some of them after review, but I think they're very useful until we decide on an approach. <!--Describe the documentation added.--> #### Documentation Updated README and the config schema.
signals.author: swiatekm

signals.title: [chore] Fix inverted IsEmpty godoc for SpanID/TraceID/ProfileID
signals.text: #### Description The unexported `IsEmpty()` helpers in `pdata/internal` for SpanID, TraceID, and ProfileID had doc comments that stated the inverse of the actual behavior, and two of them misspelled "least" as "leas". `IsEmpty()` returns true when the id is all-zero (empty), but the comments said it returns true when the id "contains at least one non-zero byte". This aligns the three internal comments to the wording already used by the correct public twins in `pdata/pcommon` and `pdata/pprofile`. #### Link to tracking issue No tracking issue. This is a comment-only doc fix (3 lines); the public copies are the canonical wording, so the correct text is self-evident. Under 20 changed lines, so it is exempt from the linked-issue requirement. #### Testing None added. This is a comment-only change with no behavior change. `go build ./internal/...`, `gofmt`, and `go test ./internal/` pass. #### Documentation Comment-only godoc correction; no documentation files changed. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

[#​3973](https://redirect.github.com/github/codeql-action/pull/3973) </details> <details> <summary>lycheeverse/lychee-action (lycheeverse/lychee-action)</summary> ### [`v2.9.0`](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/releases/tag/v2.9.0) [Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/compare/v2.8.0...v2.9.0) #### Summary This release updates the default lychee version from `v0.23.0` to `v0.24.2`. The main reason for this release is compatibility with the new lychee `0.24.x` release artifacts. Starting with lychee `v0.24.0`, the archive layout changed, and the `lychee` binary may now be packaged inside a subdirectory. `lychee-action` now detects that layout automatically, so users can upgrade without changing their workflows. If you use: ```yaml uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2 ``` you will get the new version once the floating `v2` tag has been updated. If you pin exact versions, update to: ```yaml uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2.9.0 ``` #### What’s new from lychee `v0.24.x` ##### Better diagnostics lychee now reports line and column numbers for detected links. This makes broken link reports easier to act on, especially in larger documentation sites or generated reports. ##### Text fragment checking lychee can now check URL text fragments, such as links containing `#:~:text=...`. This helps catch links that point to a valid page but no longer points to the intended highlighted text. ##### Sitemap support lychee can now read `sitemap.xml` inputs. This is useful for checking published websites or generated documentation sites where the sitemap is the easiest source of URLs to validate. ##### JUnit output lychee now supports JUnit output. This makes it easier to integrate link checking results with CI systems and test reporting tools that understand JUnit XML. ##### Redirect and remap visibility lychee can now show redirects and remaps more clearly. This helps explain why a URL was checked as a different final URL and makes debugging link-checking behavior easier. ##### Multiple config files lychee now supports multiple configuration files and expanded config handling. This is useful for repositories that split documentation, website, or package-specific link-checking settings. ##### Timeout handling lychee can now accept timeouts explicitly. This gives users more control over how strict their link checks should be for flaky or slow endpoints. #### Fixes and reliability improvements ##### Fixed lychee `0.24.x` archive compatibility `lychee-action` now handles the new lychee release archive layout by detecting whether the `lychee` binary is inside a subdirectory. This fixes compatibility with lychee `0.24.x`. ##### More stable installation path The action now installs lychee into `$RUNNER_TEMP/lychee/bin` instead of `$HOME`. This avoids failures on runners where `$HOME` differs between composite action steps. In those environments, the action could add one directory to `PATH` but install the binary somewhere else, causing `lychee: command not found`. ##### Safer automatic lychee version updates The workflow that checks for new lychee releases now guards against `null` release versions before creating update PRs. This prevents invalid automated PRs such as “Update lycheeVersion to null”. ##### Dependency updates - Updated `actions/checkout` from `v6` to `v7` - Updated `actions/cache` from `v5` to `v6` #### Upstream lychee changelog For the full lychee changelog, see: - signals.title: [exporterhelper] Cache request size per sizer type
signals.text: **Fixes #12636** ## Description When the batcher is configured with `sizer: bytes`, `partitionBatcher.consumeInternal` decides whether to flush by calling `qb.sizer.Sizeof(currentBatch)` → `req.BytesSize()` on every consumed request. `BytesSize()` ignored the cached size and recomputed the serialized protobuf size of the **entire accumulated batch** each time (`plog.ProtoMarshaler.LogsSize`, which walks every attribute of every record). Because the batch grows toward `min_size` as requests are merged, this makes accumulation **O(n²)** in the number of merged requests. With a large `min_size` (e.g. 32 MiB) and many small requests, `BytesSize`/`SizeProto` dominates CPU — we observed it at ~86% of one of our log writing component using exporter queue batching on-CPU time in production, starving the consumer and backing up the sending queue. `MergeSplit` already maintains the size incrementally and cheaply, but that cached value was thrown away by the separate `BytesSize()` accessor. A single untyped `cachedSize` cannot simply back `BytesSize()`, because the batcher and the queue may ask for different sizer types (bytes vs items) on the same request — this is the correctness concern in #12636. ## Change Cache the size **per sizer dimension** — two `int` fields (`cachedItemsSize`, `cachedBytesSize`, `-1` = unset) on `logsRequest`/`tracesRequest`/`metricsRequest`, matching the maintainer's earlier "2 values, not a map" preference. `size()`, `BytesSize()`, and `ItemsCount()` read/populate the matching field; `mergeTo`/`split` maintain the dimension they use and invalidate the other (which they did not update), so a stale value is never returned. No new allocations — two ints on an existing struct. ## Benchmark New `BenchmarkByteSizeFlushCheckManySmallLogs` mirrors the batcher's per-consume MinSize check (merge a small request into the batch, then read the batch's byte size), accumulating 1000 requests: | | ns/op | allocs/op | |---|---|---| | before (single, uncached `BytesSize`) | ~121,000,000 | 71,080 | | after (per-sizer cache) | ~2,580,000 | 71,080 | ~47× faster, same allocations. Existing `./internal/...` tests pass; `gofmt` clean.

signals.title: [processor/batch] Honor Shutdown context during final flush
signals.text: On shutdown, the batch processor flushed pending data with a background-derived export context, so a cancelled or timed-out `Shutdown(ctx)` could not unblock a stuck downstream export. Store the Shutdown context before signaling workers, and use it (with shard client metadata preserved) for exports after shutdown starts. Removes the long-standing TODO in `batch_processor.go`. this PR has no corresponding dedicated issue; resolves an in-code TODO. (Happy to open one if preferred) - `TestBatchProcessorShutdownCancelsFinalFlush` - `TestBatchProcessorShutdownFinalFlushHonorsDeadline` - `TestBatchProcessorShutdownFinalFlushPreservesMetadata` - Full `go test ./processor/batchprocessor` fixes: `// TODO: Set a timeout on sendTraces or // make it cancellable using the context that Shutdown gets as a parameter` (i went with the second option I did not invent a fixed timeout inside the batch processor (e.g. always “FLUSSH for 5s”). What I did: - Save Shutdown(ctx) - Use that ctx for the final flush export - So if the caller cancels or sets a deadline/timeout on that context, the flush can unblock ) #### documentation added: Changelog entry: `.chloggen/batchprocessor-shutdown-context-final-flush.yaml` #### Providing authorships I have written this PR description myself, a human being.

signals.title: Add recursion depth limit to JSON unmarshalling
signals.text: #### Description The proto unmarshal path bounds recursion depth to guard against stack exhaustion from deeply nested payloads, but the JSON path had no equivalent limit. An `AnyValue` whose value is an `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` of `AnyValue`s, nested deeply enough, recurses through the generated `UnmarshalJSON` methods until the goroutine stack overflows — a fatal, unrecoverable crash (`recover()` cannot catch it), not just a failed request. It's reachable through the public `JSONUnmarshaler` from any component that decodes untrusted OTLP/JSON without a request-size cap. This tracks nesting depth on the JSON `Iterator` (`EnterRecursive`/`ExitRecursive`, with a limit of 100) and injects the guard at the top of every generated `UnmarshalJSON` via the pdatagen template, so over-limit nesting returns an error instead of overflowing the stack. This mirrors the proto side (#15597). The limit sits well beyond any realistic telemetry nesting — the effective budget is ~47 nested `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` levels, matching the proto path — so well-formed payloads are unaffected. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15603 #### Testing - Added `TestUnmarshalJSONLogsRecursionLimit`: shallow nesting still succeeds; nesting past the limit now returns an error rather than being accepted (previously it was accepted, and at larger depths crashed the process with `fatal error: stack overflow`). - Full `pdata` module `go test ./...` passes; `golangci-lint` clean on the changed packages. - Regenerated code is guard-only (each generated `UnmarshalJSON` gains the same 4-line entry check) and `make genpdata` is idempotent. #### Documentation No user-facing documentation changes; a `.chloggen` entry (`bug_fix`, `pkg/pdata`) is included. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

signals.title: [pdata/pprofile] Use the ProfilesDictionary for attributes in OTLP export requests
signals.text: #### Description On the OTLP export path, `pprofileotlp.ExportRequest` serialized its payload directly instead of going through the `pprofile` marshalers, so Resource attributes were not converted to references in the `ProfilesDictionary`. It now delegates to `pprofile.ProtoMarshaler/JSONMarshaler` and their unmarshalers. Doing that exposed a bug in `resolveKeyValueReferences`: an unset `key_strindex` was treated as a reference to `string_table[0]` (ie. ""), so attribute keys sent inline were silently erased. `key_strindex` is also now cleared once resolved, so resolved attributes no longer carry both `key` and `key_strindex` since the optimization that justified it was removed in #15134. Fixing `key_strindex == 0` handling also uncovered another issue: if `pprofile.ProtoMarshaler` is called on a profile with an empty string table, the first interned string lands at index 0. So the attribute key is lost on unmarshal and the emitted string_table violates string_table[0] MUST be "". Interning now inserts the sentinel when the string table is empty. Note that it is unclear whose responsibility it is to insert the sentinel: `NewProfiles()` does not add it, and `pprofile.SetString` returns index 0 for the first string added to an empty table. <!-- Issue number if applicable --> #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15792 Fixes #15793 <!--Describe what testing was performed and which tests were added.--> #### Testing New helper `requireProfilesEqualIgnoringAppendedStrings` was added in three places (pb_test.go, request_test.go, otlp_test.go). It exists because the round trip is no longer an identity on the dictionary: marshaling interns attribute strings into the string table, and unmarshaling inlines them again without pruning, so `got`'s table is `want`'s plus an unused tail. The helper truncates `got`'s table to `want`'s length and compares everything else exactly. It's duplicated rather than shared because the three call sites are in two modules and three packages, and one of them is an in-package test of `pprofile` itself. Sharing it would mean a new public API in `pdata/pprofile`. The mdatagen fixtures have been replaced by valid profiles: `GenTestProfilesDictionary` yields `StringTable = []string{"", "test_stringtable"}` and one dummy entry per table, with indices that don't refer to anything. That was ok when the marshalers ignored the dictionary but now that they intern and resolve references, valid profiles are needed to correctly test that attributes that can be interned and resolved consistently. `MarkReadOnly()` was added in all three files: the marshalers mutate their input while interning unless it's read-only, in which case they copy first. Without it the input is rewritten by the marshal and the later comparison is meaningless. Tests added - TestResolveProfilesReferencesWithInlineKey (dictionary_helpers_test.go): unit-level, fails on the old >= 0 guard Tests modified - TestProfilesProtoWireCompatibility (pb_test.go): pdata-level comparison restored in place of the wire3/goproto.Equal block - TestProfilesProtoWireCompatibility (request_test.go): now exercises the delegating marshalers <!--Describe the documentation added.--> #### Documentation <!--Authorship attestation. See AGENTS.md for details. AI agents must not check this box on behalf of the user; the human author must check it themselves before the PR is ready for review.--> #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself. <!--Please delete paragraphs that you did not use before submitting.--> ##### Related The gRPC path is left unchanged but it likely needs fixing as well, at minimum to resolve references on the receiving side.

signals.title: fix: bound memory growth in queuebatch split path by flushing incrementally [fj4WqyCCw3C5ShR1RfB7MoBPTpkRrBFYP1uT35g3MvT]
signals.text: **Fixes #15747** **Problem:** `consumeInternal` in `partition_batcher.go` calls `MergeSplit` which eagerly builds the entire chunk list upfront. When all flush workers are occupied by a slow exporter, the `Consume` goroutine stalls on the first `flush()` call while every remaining chunk — each a freshly allocated `plog.Logs` / `ptrace.Traces` / `pmetric.Metrics` — stays live and reachable, **uncounted by `queue_size` or any other bound**. This can lead to unbounded memory growth (RSS exceeding 200GB in production, 36GB+ heap snapshots in the `split` → `extractLogs` → `plog.NewLogs` call chain). **Root cause:** `split()` eagerly builds the entire chunk list before returning. `flush()` blocks until a worker is free. When every `num_consumers` worker is occupied by a slow produce call, the loop stalls on chunk 0 while every remaining chunk stays live. **Fix:** - Add a `SplitOne` method to `logsRequest`, `tracesRequest`, and `metricsRequest` that splits off **one chunk at a time** from the request, leaving the remainder in the receiver. - Add an optional `splitOne` interface in `partition_batcher.go` (Go type-assertion pattern, no change to the `request.Request` interface). - Add `consumeSplitLoop` that calls `SplitOne` in a loop, flushing each chunk immediately, so only **one chunk at a time** is live in memory (plus the worker pool's in-flight chunks). - Add `AddRef` to `refCountDone` to support dynamic ref-counting when the total number of chunks is not known upfront. **Memory bound:** With lazy splitting, at most `num_consumers + 1` chunks are live at any time, instead of the full request-size / max-size count. **Backward compatibility:** - The `splitOne` interface is optional; existing `Request` implementations (e.g. `FakeRequest` in tests) continue to use the eager `MergeSplit` path, unchanged. - All existing tests pass without modification. **Testing:** - Manual: verified each chunk is ≤ maxSize, total item count preserved, remainder handling matches eager path. - CI: all existing `partition_batcher_test.go` tests pass (use `FakeRequest` which doesn't implement `splitOne`). signal.title: [exporterhelper] ObsMetrics interfaces for queue/batch behavior
signal.text: #### Description This enables non-exporter components such as `queuebatchprocessor` to expose exporterhelper metrics in processor-specific ways. Half of the prototype https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/pull/15770, other half is #15802. There are three levels of interface: the queue, the batch, and the exporterhelper module itself. | Level | Sync | Async | Instrument kinds | |---|---:|---:|---| | Queue | 3 | 2 | 1 counter, 2 histograms, 2 observable gauges | | Batch | 2 | 0 | 2 histograms | | Exporterhelper | 3 | 0 | 2 counters, 1 up/down counter | The interface has fewer methods because item and byte histograms share one callback: • QueueMetrics: 2 synchronous recording methods and 2 asynchronous observer-registration methods • QueueBatchMetrics: 1 synchronous recording method • ObsMetrics: 3 synchronous recording methods plus Shutdown. Part of https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/docs/rfcs/batching-migration.md #### Link to tracking issue Part of #14038 #### Testing ✅ #### Documentation ✅ #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.
signal.author: jmacd

signal.title: [chore][rfc/confmap]: add two new approaches for merging lists across configurations
signal.text: Following up on my meeting with @mx-psi, @dmitryax and @evan-bradley, I'm adding two more approaches we discussed during the meet for `docs/rfcs/configuration-merging-strategy.md`. 1. Specifying the lists to merge via command line flags: - This approach adds separate top-level CLI flags to control the merging behaviour. 2. Specifying the lists to merge in the configuration itself: - This approac uses a dedicated top-level `merge:` section that declares which paths in *that file* should be merged into the running configuration

signal.title: fix: bound memory growth in queuebatch split path by flushing incrementally [fj4WqyCCw3C5ShR1RfB7MoBPTpkRrBFYP1uT35g3MvT]
signal.text: **Fixes #15747** **Problem:** `consumeInternal` in `partition_batcher.go` calls `MergeSplit` which eagerly builds the entire chunk list upfront. When all flush workers are occupied by a slow exporter, the `Consume` goroutine stalls on the first `flush()` call while every remaining chunk — each a freshly allocated `plog.Logs` / `ptrace.Traces` / `pmetric.Metrics` — stays live and reachable, **uncounted by `queue_size` or any other bound**. This can lead to unbounded memory growth (RSS exceeding 200GB in production, 36GB+ heap snapshots in the `split` → `extractLogs` → `plog.NewLogs` call chain). **Root cause:** `split()` eagerly builds the entire chunk list before returning. `flush()` blocks until a worker is free. When every `num_consumers` worker is occupied by a slow produce call, the loop stalls on chunk 0 while every remaining chunk stays live. **Fix:** - Add a `SplitOne` method to `logsRequest`, `tracesRequest`, and `metricsRequest` that splits off **one chunk at a time** from the request, leaving the remainder in the receiver. - Add an optional `splitOne` interface in `partition_batcher.go` (Go type-assertion pattern, no change to the `request.Request` interface). - Add `consumeSplitLoop` that calls `SplitOne` in a loop, flushing each chunk immediately, so only **one chunk at a time** is live in memory (plus the worker pool's in-flight chunks). - Add `AddRef` to `refCountDone` to support dynamic ref-counting when the total number of chunks is not known upfront. **Memory bound:** With lazy splitting, at most `num_consumers + 1` chunks are live at any time, instead of the full request-size / max-size count. **Backward compatibility:** - The `splitOne` interface is optional; existing `Request` implementations (e.g. `FakeRequest` in tests) continue to use the eager `MergeSplit` path, unchanged. - All existing tests pass without modification. **Testing:** - Manual: verified each chunk is ≤ maxSize, total item count preserved, remainder handling matches eager path. - CI: all existing `partition_batcher_test.go` tests pass (use `FakeRequest` which doesn't implement `splitOne`). signal.title: Add queue-oriented storage interface for persistent queues
signal.text: ### Component(s) exporter/exporterhelper ### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe. When setting up persistent queues, we use `file_storage` as the mechanism to store in-flight data. This is backed by a bbolt database. [Like others](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/44469), we have had stability issues caused by excessive bbolt memory usage when using this configuration. Our main issue occurs at startup when queues are large (100GB+), but there are various incarnations of the problem where bbolt will use excessive memory, leading to OOMKills. When trying to build our own replacement that does not use bbolt, we quickly ran into a design issue preventing resolution of the problem. The current [storage.Client](https://pkg.go.dev/go.opentelemetry.io/collector/extension/xextension/storage#section-readme) interface used for persistent queuing is key/value oriented. When implementing a storage provider, one must support random access by key. This design requires a storage provider to have some form of indexing (to efficiently find the key) and a data structure that can support random sets and deletes by key. With queues that may exceed 100GB (the need for these large queues is out of our control), indexing not only requires extra disk and reduces performance, but its also unnecessary. We'd simply like to store events in a FIFO-like queue and retrieve them later. As an added benefit, FIFO operations would be roughly constant time and would not get slower as the queue increases in size. ### Describe the solution you'd like In addition to the current key/value interface, I'd like to propose a secondary interface that implements a proper queue abstraction. Rather than get/set/delete, we'd use a FIFO interface. To illustrate the concept at a high level, this would be something like: ```go type QueueClient interface { Close(ctx context.Context) error // Offer appends one item to the durable tail of the queue. Offer(ctx context.Context, value []byte) error // Reserve claims the next item from the durable head of the queue for // processing. The item remains durable until Ack is called with the returned // ID. If the process crashes or the reservation expires, the item should // become eligible for reservation again. Reserve(ctx context.Context, lease LeaseOptions) (QueueEntryID, []byte, error) // Ack permanently completes a reserved item. Ack(ctx context.Context, id QueueEntryID) error // Nack releases a reserved item back to the queue without completing it. Nack(ctx context.Context, id QueueEntryID) error } ``` Under the hood, we'd write the events to segmented files. Once all the events in a segment have been acked, we'd reclaim that segment. ### Describe alternatives you've considered It may be possible to implement an on-disk queue and use sqlite or something for key to queue entry ID bookkeeping, but introducing a queue-oriented extension interface avoids the additional overhead associated with that mapping. ### Additional context _No response_ ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

signal.title: queuestorage: A storage extension optimized for queues based on bbolt.
signal.text: ### Component(s) exporter/exporterhelper ### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe. For exporterhelper queue, we have filestorage extension which has multiple performance issue like Process Memory shootup and high disk i/o consumption by bbolt DB when queue size is large. These are the same issues already listed in https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/15384 and https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/44469 . ### Describe the solution you'd like An enhanced version of bbolt which is purely optimized for queue use case. All performance issues arises when bbolt database gets large and b-tree and mmap grows. We can use segmented access pattern. Since it's for queue based extension, say queue_storage extension where we know we know that we don't need all keys to be loaded by bbolt, since we know queue consumption will be sequential, we can leverage that to create sequential segment db files. Segment-per-bbolt design Example: When say, 64MB is the segment limit. This can be made configurable. ``` storage-dir/ seg_000000000000.db ← oldest active segment (items 0–1000 , sizne ~64MB) seg_000000001000.db ← next segment (items 1000–1999, size ~64MB) seg_000000002000.db ← current write segment (...) qmv0 metadata key same as existing filestorage. ``` Each seg_*.db is a normal bbolt database, but holds only the items for that slice of the queue. The filename encodes the starting write index of that segment so you can route any key to its segment in O(1). In reality, we need to open a new segment DB file only after consuming all items for previous segment. Also we would need to open 2 segment files at any time , one to enqueue(most latest segment file) and one to dequeue(Can be any from segment file which is actively being read..). In this way, otel process will open atmost 2 segment DB files at anytime even for a very large queue backlog. This makes memory config/growth very predictable(~124MB for 2 segment files). Also since a single read segment loaded is memory bounded(64Mb default), we can reduce random disk access by preloading the 64MB data pages sequentially into OS cache and when bbolt needs a ramdom page traversing B-tree index, it finds it in OS cache rather than making a Disk i/o. This concept is tested in below attached doc and an impressive ~8x read speed improvement and reduced disk iops was observed. This feature request is a fork from https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/15384#issuecomment-5100729005 I have implemented the same to do a POC and capture the testing and performance benchmarks in [this doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TsrdIhJpU2kica8rsA8nnQaYUVvPr11F7Z_QqjGkO80/edit?tab=t.0) [Draft implementation](https://github.com/jagan2221/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/extension/storage/queuestorage) of queuestorage extension. This implementation contains the core implementations for now for doing a POC. Cosmetic changes and config related things like ensuring all the required configs and defaults are yet to be done based on approval. **List of performance related issue we have with filestorage extension vs How segmented approach solves this.** **Segmented BBolt vs Single BBolt — Improvements Summary** **1. Bounded Memory Usage** Single DB mmaps the entire file — a 50GB queue means 50GB of virtual memory pressure, leading to OOM kills under memory limits. Segmented approach only mmaps 2-3 open segments (128-192 MiB) regardless of total queue size. **2. Instant Space Reclamation** In single DB, deleted items remain as freelist pages — the file never shrinks without expensive compaction. In segmented, once all items in a segment are acked, os.Remove() deletes the file instantly. Disk space is freed in real-time as consumers catch up. **3. Fast Startup** Single DB must reconstruct the freelist by scanning the entire B-tree on open — 30GB file takes 30-60 seconds. Segmented opens only 1 segment file (~100ms) and reads metadata. Startup time is constant regardless of queue history. **4. Low Disk I/O Thrashing** A 64MB segment fits entirely in the OS page cache. All reads within a segment are memory accesses with zero page faults. Single large DB's B-tree index pages are scattered across the entire file and get evicted under memory pressure, causing 5-6 random IOPs per read. **5. No Compaction Overhead** Single DB requires periodic compaction to reclaim space — this copies the entire live dataset to a new file, consuming heavy CPU, IOPS, and temporary disk space (2x). Segmented never needs compaction — segment deletion is the GC mechanism. Zero background CPU, zero IOPS wasted on maintenance. **6. Predictable Tail Latency** Compaction in single DB causes latency spikes (write stalls while DB is being copied/reopened). Segmented has no such stalls — every operation has consistent latency since there's no background maintenance competing for resources. **7. Better IOPS Budget Utilization** For IOPS bounded machines, Like a VM running on AWS with gp3 (3000 IOPS baseline) for storage, single DB startup can saturate the entire IOPS budget for 30-60 seconds (scanning freelist). Segmented startup consumes less IOPs. ### Describe alternatives you've considered Wanted to try a different DB like pebble, which is as LSM based storage, but initial thoughts about the use case which is data written will be deleted very quickly and new data will be enqueued. this kind of high throughtput short lived data could potentially be expensive because of tombstones and old SSTables eventually need compaction. Also when thought about enhancing bbolt, i felt enhanced bbolt will perform much better to address the performance limitations which we have currently given it's already time tested with filestorage extension. ### Additional context _No response_ ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

signal.title: [confighttp] Move keepalive config into a dedicated optional section
signal.text: #### Description Move the keepalive-related options into a dedicated optional section. We go from: ```yaml endpoint: "http://localhost:4318" idle_conn_timeout: 90s max_idle_conns: 100 max_idle_conns_per_host: 10 ``` to: ```yaml endpoint: "http://localhost:4318" keepalive: idle_conn_timeout: 90s max_idle_conns: 100 max_idle_conns_per_host: 10 ``` The old configuration still exists and works. We fail validation if both are set. The implementation is somewhat complex and tries to minimize breakage across multiple scenarios. It proceeds by standardizing on the old, deprecated fields in `Unmarshal` and nulling the new section. See comments on the `Unmarshal` implementation and compatibility tests in `keepalive_compat_tests.go`. The most notable scenario that doesn't work goes like this: ```go cfg := NewDefaultClientConfig() conf.Unmarshal(cfg) cfg.KeepAlive = nil client := cfg.ToClient() ``` Keepalives will be enabled for such a client. This, and other limitations, exist as tests in `keepalive_compat_test.go`. Their intent is to show how a given implementation fares, in case somebody can come up with a better one. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/14020 #### Testing Added unit tests for all the new functions and some more generic unmarshalling tests. I've also added compatibility tests in `keepalive_compat_test.go` which assert that typical use cases from contrib still work as expected, and also show the limitations of this approach. I'm open to dropping some of them after review, but I think they're very useful until we decide on an approach. <!--Describe the documentation added.--> #### Documentation Updated README and the config schema.

signal.title: [pdata/pprofile] Use the ProfilesDictionary for attributes in OTLP export requests
signal.text: #### Description On the OTLP export path, `pprofileotlp.ExportRequest` serialized its payload directly instead of going through the `pprofile` marshalers, so Resource attributes were not converted to references in the `ProfilesDictionary`. It now delegates to `pprofile.ProtoMarshaler/JSONMarshaler` and their unmarshalers. Doing that exposed a bug in `resolveKeyValueReferences`: an unset `key_strindex` was treated as a reference to `string_table[0]` (ie. ""), so attribute keys sent inline were silently erased. `key_strindex` is also now cleared once resolved, so resolved attributes no longer carry both `key` and `key_strindex` since the optimization that justified it was removed in #15134. Fixing `key_strindex == 0` handling also uncovered another issue: if `pprofile.ProtoMarshaler` is called on a profile with an empty string table, the first interned string lands at index 0. So the attribute key is lost on unmarshal and the emitted string_table violates string_table[0] MUST be "". Interning now inserts the sentinel when the string table is empty. Note that it is unclear whose responsibility it is to insert the sentinel: `NewProfiles()` does not add it, and `pprofile.SetString` returns index 0 for the first string added to an empty table. <!-- Issue number if applicable --> #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15792 Fixes #15793 <!--Describe what testing was performed and which tests were added.--> #### Testing New helper `requireProfilesEqualIgnoringAppendedStrings` was added in three places (pb_test.go, request_test.go, otlp_test.go). It exists because the round trip is no longer an identity on the dictionary: marshaling interns attribute strings into the string table, and unmarshaling inlines them again without pruning, so `got`'s table is `want`'s plus an unused tail. The helper truncates `got`'s table to `want`'s length and compares everything else exactly. It's duplicated rather than shared because the three call sites are in two modules and three packages, and one of them is an in-package test of `pprofile` itself. Sharing it would mean a new public API in `pdata/pprofile`. The mdatagen fixtures have been replaced by valid profiles: `GenTestProfilesDictionary` yields `StringTable = []string{"", "test_stringtable"}` and one dummy entry per table, with indices that don't refer to anything. That was ok when the marshalers ignored the dictionary but now that they intern and resolve references, valid profiles are needed to correctly test that attributes that can be interned and resolved consistently. `MarkReadOnly()` was added in all three files: the marshalers mutate their input while interning unless it's read-only, in which case they copy first. Without it the input is rewritten by the marshal and the later comparison is meaningless. Tests added - TestResolveProfilesReferencesWithInlineKey (dictionary_helpers_test.go): unit-level, fails on the old >= 0 guard Tests modified - TestProfilesProtoWireCompatibility (pb_test.go): pdata-level comparison restored in place of the wire3/goproto.Equal block - TestProfilesProtoWireCompatibility (request_test.go): now exercises the delegating marshalers <!--Describe the documentation added.--> #### Documentation <!--Authorship attestation. signal.title: Unset key_strindex is treated as a reference to string_table[0], erasing inline attribute keys
signal.text: ### Component(s) pdata/pprofile ### What happened? **Describe the bug** `resolveKeyValueReferences` in `pdata/pprofile/dictionary_helpers.go` treats `key_strindex == 0` as a valid reference: ```go if kv.KeyStrindex >= 0 { idx := int(kv.KeyStrindex) if idx < dict.StringTable().Len() { kv.Key = dict.StringTable().At(idx) ``` But `0` is the "not set" sentinel, so for any producer that sends attribute keys inline the key is silently replaced with `""` on unmarshal. **Steps to reproduce** ```go msg := &profilesv1.ProfilesData{ ResourceProfiles: []*profilesv1.ResourceProfiles{{ Resource: &resourcev1.Resource{Attributes: []*commonv1.KeyValue{{ Key: "service.name", Value: &commonv1.AnyValue{Value: &commonv1.AnyValue_StringValue{StringValue: "checkout"}}, }}}, ScopeProfiles: []*profilesv1.ScopeProfiles{{}}, }}, Dictionary: &profilesv1.ProfilesDictionary{StringTable: []string{""}}, } wire, _ := proto.Marshal(msg) pd, _ := (&pprofile.ProtoUnmarshaler{}).UnmarshalProfiles(wire) fmt.Println(pd.ResourceProfiles().At(0).Resource().Attributes().AsRaw()) ``` **What did you expect to see?** `map[service.name:checkout]` **What did you see instead?** `map[:checkout]`: the attribute key is gone. ### Collector version v0.159.0 ### Environment information _No response_ ### OpenTelemetry Collector configuration ```yaml ``` ### Log output ```shell ``` ### Additional context Related: `key_strindex` is also not cleared after resolution. The code intentionally keeps it set ("N.b. keep KeyStrindex set to optimize re-marshaling. This is technically a violation of the proto spec"), but this seems dangerous: any serialization path that does not run `convertKeyValueToReferences` emits both fileds onto the wire. `pprofileotlp.ExportRequest.MarshalProto` is such a path (see #15792). Moreover the optimization that jusitified this has been removed by #15134. ### Tip <sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

signal.title: pprofileotlp.ExportRequest does not use the ProfilesDictionary for Resource attributes
signal.text: ### Component(s) pdata/pprofile ### What happened? **Describe the bug** `pprofileotlp.ExportRequest` serializes `ms.orig` directly rather than delegating to the `pprofile` marshalers: ```go func (ms ExportRequest) MarshalProto() ([]byte, error) { size := ms.orig.SizeProto() buf := make([]byte, size) _ = ms.orig.MarshalProto(buf) return buf, nil } ``` So `convertProfilesToReferences` never runs on marshal, and `resolveProfilesReferences` never runs on unmarshal (same for the JSON pair). The reference-based attribute support added in #14546 therefore does not apply on the OTLP export path, the path the OTLP receiver and exporter actually use. **Steps to reproduce** ```go pd := pprofile.NewProfiles() pd.Dictionary().StringTable().Append("") // index 0 must be the empty sentinel rp := pd.ResourceProfiles().AppendEmpty() rp.Resource().Attributes().PutStr("service.name", "checkout") rp.ScopeProfiles().AppendEmpty() pd.MarkReadOnly() // so the first marshal copies instead of mutating pd viaPprofile, _ := (&pprofile.ProtoMarshaler{}).MarshalProfiles(pd) viaExportReq, _ := pprofileotlp.NewExportRequestFromProfiles(pd).MarshalProto() var a profilesv1.ProfilesData proto.Unmarshal(viaPprofile, &a) var b collectorprofilesv1.ExportProfilesServiceRequest proto.Unmarshal(viaExportReq, &b) fmt.Printf("pprofile.ProtoMarshaler string_table=%q (%d bytes)\n", a.GetDictionary().GetStringTable(), len(viaPprofile)) fmt.Printf("ExportRequest.MarshalProto string_table=%q (%d bytes)\n", b.GetDictionary().GetStringTable(), len(viaExportReq)) ``` **What did you expect to see?** Both encodings referencing the attribute key and string value through the dictionary string table. **What did you see instead?** ``` pprofile.ProtoMarshaler string_table=["" "service.name" "checkout"] (44 bytes) ExportRequest.MarshalProto string_table=[""] (40 bytes) ``` The `ExportRequest` encoding leaves string_table untouched and inlines the attribute (`key="service.name"`, k`ey_strindex=0`). Two marshalers of the same `Profiles` produce different wire encodings, and the dictionary wire-size benefit is lost on the export path. ### Collector version v0.159.0

signal.title: [pdata/pprofile] add bounds checks to FromLocationIndices and switchDictionary
signal.text: #### Description Follow-up to #15517, which added bounds checks to `FromAttributeIndices`. The same untrusted-input crash survived in two sibling paths: `FromLocationIndices` had no bounds check at all, and the five `switchDictionary` loops checked only the upper bound, letting a negative index reach `At(-1)`. `FromLocationIndices` gains an error return, mirroring what #15517 did to `FromAttributeIndices`, including the message shape. It has no production callers in core or contrib, so the signature change is contained to this package's own tests. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15697 #### Testing Added out-of-bounds and negative cases to `TestFromLocationIndices`, and a negative-index case to each of the five `switchDictionary` tests. Each new case panics without the corresponding guard. `go test -race` passes for `pdata/pprofile` and the whole `pdata` module. #### Documentation Changelog entry (`change_type: breaking`, `component: pkg/pprofile`, `change_logs: [user, api]`). #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

signal.title: [exporterhelper] Cache request size per sizer type
signal.text: **Fixes #12636** ## Description When the batcher is configured with `sizer: bytes`, `partitionBatcher.consumeInternal` decides whether to flush by calling `qb.sizer.Sizeof(currentBatch)` → `req.BytesSize()` on every consumed request. `BytesSize()` ignored the cached size and recomputed the serialized protobuf size of the **entire accumulated batch** each time (`plog.ProtoMarshaler.LogsSize`, which walks every attribute of every record). Because the batch grows toward `min_size` as requests are merged, this makes accumulation **O(n²)** in the number of merged requests. With a large `min_size` (e.g. 32 MiB) and many small requests, `BytesSize`/`SizeProto` dominates CPU — we observed it at ~86% of one of our log writing component using exporter queue batching on-CPU time in production, starving the consumer and backing up the sending queue. `MergeSplit` already maintains the size incrementally and cheaply, but that cached value was thrown away by the separate `BytesSize()` accessor. A single untyped `cachedSize` cannot simply back `BytesSize()`, because the batcher and the queue may ask for different sizer types (bytes vs items) on the same request — this is the correctness concern in #12636. ## Change Cache the size **per sizer dimension** — two `int` fields (`cachedItemsSize`, `cachedBytesSize`, `-1` = unset) on `logsRequest`/`tracesRequest`/`metricsRequest`, matching the maintainer's earlier "2 values, not a map" preference. `size()`, `BytesSize()`, and `ItemsCount()` read/populate the matching field; `mergeTo`/`split` maintain the dimension they use and invalidate the other (which they did not update), so a stale value is never returned. No new allocations — two ints on an existing struct. ## Benchmark New `BenchmarkByteSizeFlushCheckManySmallLogs` mirrors the batcher's per-consume MinSize check (merge a small request into the batch, then read the batch's byte size), accumulating 1000 requests: | | ns/op | allocs/op | |---|---|---| | before (single, uncached `BytesSize`) | ~121,000,000 | 71,080 | | after (per-sizer cache) | ~2,580,000 | 71,080 | ~47× faster, same allocations. Existing `./internal/...` tests pass; `gofmt` clean.

signal.title: [processor/batch] Honor Shutdown context during final flush
signal.text: On shutdown, the batch processor flushed pending data with a background-derived export context, so a cancelled or timed-out `Shutdown(ctx)` could not unblock a stuck downstream export. Store the Shutdown context before signaling workers, and use it (with shard client metadata preserved) for exports after shutdown starts. Removes the long-standing TODO in `batch_processor.go`. this PR has no corresponding dedicated issue; resolves an in-code TODO. (Happy to open one if preferred) - `TestBatchProcessorShutdownCancelsFinalFlush` - `TestBatchProcessorShutdownFinalFlushHonorsDeadline` - `TestBatchProcessorShutdownFinalFlushPreservesMetadata` - Full `go test ./processor/batchprocessor` fixes: `// TODO: Set a timeout on sendTraces or // make it cancellable using the context that Shutdown gets as a parameter` (i went with the second option I did not invent a fixed timeout inside the batch processor (e.g. always “FLUSSH for 5s”). What I did: - Save Shutdown(ctx) - Use that ctx for the final flush export - So if the caller cancels or sets a deadline/timeout on that context, the flush can unblock ) #### documentation added: Changelog entry: `.chloggen/batchprocessor-shutdown-context-final-flush.yaml` #### Providing authorships I have written this PR description myself, a human being.

signal.title: Add recursion depth limit to JSON unmarshalling
signal.text: #### Description The proto unmarshal path bounds recursion depth to guard against stack exhaustion from deeply nested payloads, but the JSON path had no equivalent limit. An `AnyValue` whose value is an `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` of `AnyValue`s, nested deeply enough, recurses through the generated `UnmarshalJSON` methods until the goroutine stack overflows — a fatal, unrecoverable crash (`recover()` cannot catch it), not just a failed request. It's reachable through the public `JSONUnmarshaler` from any component that decodes untrusted OTLP/JSON without a request-size cap. This tracks nesting depth on the JSON `Iterator` (`EnterRecursive`/`ExitRecursive`, with a limit of 100) and injects the guard at the top of every generated `UnmarshalJSON` via the pdatagen template, so over-limit nesting returns an error instead of overflowing the stack. This mirrors the proto side (#15597). The limit sits well beyond any realistic telemetry nesting — the effective budget is ~47 nested `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` levels, matching the proto path — so well-formed payloads are unaffected. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15603 #### Testing - Added `TestUnmarshalJSONLogsRecursionLimit`: shallow nesting still succeeds; nesting past the limit now returns an error rather than being accepted (previously it was accepted, and at larger depths crashed the process with `fatal error: stack overflow`). - Full `pdata` module `go test ./...` passes; `golangci-lint` clean on the changed packages. - Regenerated code is guard-only (each generated `UnmarshalJSON` gains the same 4-line entry check) and `make genpdata` is idempotent. #### Documentation No user-facing documentation changes; a `.chloggen` entry (`bug_fix`, `pkg/pdata`) is included. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

signal.title: fix(configtls): use correct variable in invalid curve type error message
signal.text: ## Summary - Fix error message that formats the wrong variable when an invalid TLS curve type is specified ## Bug The error message formats `curveID` (the zero value of `tls.CurveID`, i.e., `0`) instead of `curve` (the user-provided string). Users see `%!s(uint16=0)` instead of the actual invalid input. ## Fix Change `curveID` to `curve` in the error format string.
